title: How do you consume JSON in Spring Kafka (configure `JsonDeserializer` / `spring.kafka.consumer.value-deserializer` with trusted packages), what is the default deserializer, and how do you dynamically pause/resume a listener (`KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry` → `MessageListenerContainer.pause()/resume()`, e.g. to stop consuming while the DB is down)?
shortTitle: How do you consume JSON in Spring Kafka, what is the default deserializer, and how do you dynamically pause/resume a listener?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka stores values as raw bytes, so a deserializer turns those bytes back into an object. The raw client default is `ByteArrayDeserializer` and Spring's broader default via `spring.kafka.consumer.value-deserializer` is typically `StringDeserializer` unless you configure otherwise. To consume JSON into a Java type you set the value deserializer to Spring Kafka's `JsonDeserializer`, point it at the target type, and configure trusted packages so it will only deserialize into classes you allow, which is a security control against malicious type headers. To stop and start consumption at runtime you look up the container through `KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry` by listener id and call `pause()` or `resume()` on the `MessageListenerContainer`.
s1_definition.analogy: A Kafka message arrives at National Bank of India as a sealed envelope of bytes. The deserializer is the mail clerk who opens the envelope and reconstructs the actual form inside. By default the clerk just reads the raw text, but with `JsonDeserializer` the clerk knows the envelope contains a structured transfer form and rebuilds it into a proper TransferEvent object. Trusted packages is the rule that the clerk will only accept forms from approved departments, never a forged form claiming to be a different, dangerous class. Pause and resume is the manager telling the clerk to stop opening mail while the vault computer is down, and to start again once it is back, so no form is lost and nothing piles up half-processed.
s1_definition.oneliner: `JsonDeserializer` with trusted packages safely turns JSON bytes into your type, and you pause or resume a live listener through the endpoint registry when a downstream like the database is down.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka stores values as raw bytes, so a deserializer turns those bytes back into an object. The raw client default is `ByteArrayDeserializer` and Spring's broader default via `spring.kafka.consumer.value-deserializer` is typically `StringDeserializer` unless you configure otherwise. To consume JSON into a Java type you set the value deserializer to Spring Kafka's `JsonDeserializer`, point it at the target type, and configure trusted packages so it will only deserialize into classes you allow, which is a security control against malicious type headers. To stop and start consumption at runtime you look up the container through `KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry` by listener id and call `pause()` or `resume()` on the `MessageListenerContainer`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A Kafka message arrives at National Bank of India as a sealed envelope of bytes. The deserializer is the mail clerk who opens the envelope and reconstructs the actual form inside. By default the clerk just reads the raw text, but with `JsonDeserializer` the clerk knows the envelope contains a structured transfer form and rebuilds it into a proper TransferEvent object. Trusted packages is the rule that the clerk will only accept forms from approved departments, never a forged form claiming to be a different, dangerous class. Pause and resume is the manager telling the clerk to stop opening mail while the vault computer is down, and to start again once it is back, so no form is lost and nothing piles up half-processed.

**One line to remember:** `JsonDeserializer` with trusted packages safely turns JSON bytes into your type, and you pause or resume a live listener through the endpoint registry when a downstream like the database is down.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka itself is type-agnostic; it moves bytes. The consumer's value deserializer decides how those bytes become an object. The raw Kafka client's out-of-the-box default is `ByteArrayDeserializer`, and in a typical Spring Boot setup the common default you see configured is `StringDeserializer`, which gives you the JSON as a plain string that you would then parse yourself. To skip the manual parsing and get a typed object directly, you set `spring.kafka.consumer.value-deserializer` to `org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer`. Spring Kafka's `JsonDeserializer` uses Jackson under the hood, so a byte payload like `{"txnId":"TXN-1","accountId":"SAV2001","amount":20000}` is reconstructed into a `TxnEvent` instance and handed straight to your listener method.

Two configuration details matter for correctness and security. First, the deserializer needs to know the target type. You can set a default type with `spring.kafka.consumer.properties.spring.json.value.default.type=com.bank.model.TxnEvent`, or let the producer stamp the type into a message header and the deserializer read it. Second, and critically, you must configure trusted packages with `spring.kafka.consumer.properties.spring.json.trusted.packages=com.bank.model`. By default `JsonDeserializer` refuses to instantiate arbitrary classes named in a type header, because a malicious producer could otherwise ask it to construct a dangerous class; trusted packages is an allowlist. Setting it to `*` trusts everything and is a security smell in production, so you name your own packages explicitly.

A robust production setup wraps the `JsonDeserializer` inside an `ErrorHandlingDeserializer`, so that a single malformed JSON payload becomes a recoverable error that the error handler can route to a dead letter topic, rather than throwing on the consumer thread and causing the same poison record to be retried forever and block the partition. In code the key beans look like configuring the consumer factory with the delegate deserializer and the trusted packages, for example `props.put(JsonDeserializer.TRUSTED_PACKAGES, "com.bank.model")` and `props.put(JsonDeserializer.VALUE_DEFAULT_TYPE, "com.bank.model.TxnEvent")`.

Dynamic pause and resume is about flow control at runtime. Every `@KafkaListener` can be given an id, for example `@KafkaListener(id = "settlement", topics = "txn.events")`. You inject `KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry`, look up the container with `registry.getListenerContainer("settlement")`, and call `container.pause()` or `container.resume()`. When paused, the container keeps the consumer alive and keeps its partition assignment and heartbeats, so it does not trigger a rebalance, but it stops delivering records to your method. This is exactly what you want when a downstream dependency such as the database is temporarily down: you pause so you stop consuming events you cannot process, the offsets stay where they are, and when the database recovers you resume and pick up exactly where you left off with nothing lost. The senior nuance is that pausing is far better than letting the listener keep failing, because continued failures would either burn through retries, flood the dead letter topic with transient errors, or risk the consumer being kicked out of the group; pausing cleanly holds position without a rebalance. A related nuance is that pause takes effect after the current poll's records are processed, and you typically drive pause and resume from a health indicator or a circuit breaker that watches the database.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that the settlement consumer receives JSON transfer events and must both parse them safely and stop gracefully when the account database goes down.

Problem 1 — producers publish transfer events as JSON bytes, and the team was manually parsing strings with scattered Jackson calls, which was repetitive and error-prone. This is exactly what `JsonDeserializer` solves: configure it once with the target type and the listener method receives a ready-made TxnEvent object.

Problem 2 — a security reviewer warned that a compromised producer could stamp a malicious type header and trick the deserializer into constructing an unexpected class. This is exactly what trusted packages solves: the deserializer will only build classes from the bank's own approved package, rejecting anything else.

Problem 3 — during a nightly database maintenance window the database is briefly unavailable, and the consumer kept failing on every event, flooding logs and the dead letter topic with transient errors. This is exactly what pause and resume solves: a health watcher pauses the listener when the database is down so offsets freeze in place, and resumes it when the database is healthy again, processing everything from where it stopped.

The code will define a TxnEvent, a `JsonValueDeserializer` that enforces trusted packages, a `SettlementListener` whose method consumes a typed event and writes to a simulated database, a `DatabaseHealth` flag, and a `ListenerControl` that models `KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry` by pausing and resuming a container simulator based on database health. The demo step is: consume two events while the database is up, mark the database down and pause, attempt to feed more events and watch them held, bring the database back and resume, and watch the held events process cleanly in order.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE settlements (
    txn_id     VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    settled_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      # JSON deserializer wrapped for safety against poison payloads
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
        spring.json.value.default.type: com.bank.settlement.model.TxnEvent
        spring.json.trusted.packages: com.bank.settlement.model   # allowlist, NOT '*'
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four JSON transfer events on the wire, and a database that starts healthy, goes down, and recovers.

Step 1: TXN-1 arrives as JSON bytes. The deserializer confirms the target type TxnEvent lives in the trusted package, rebuilds the object with accountId SAV2001 and amount 20000, and hands it to the listener. The database is up, so the settlement is written.

Step 2: TXN-2 is deserialized the same way into Priya's event and settled, because the database is still healthy.

Step 3: The database goes down. The health watcher fires and calls pause on the container. The consumer stays alive and keeps its partition assignment and heartbeats, so there is no rebalance, but delivery to the listener method stops.

Step 4: TXN-3 and TXN-4 arrive while paused. They are held back and the committed offsets do not advance, so nothing is lost and no failed settlement is attempted against the dead database.

Step 5: The database recovers. The health watcher calls resume. The container drains the held events in their original order, settling TXN-3 for Rajesh and then TXN-4 for Priya, picking up exactly where it left off.

Step 6: The output shows two normal settlements, a pause with two held events, and a resume that flushes them in order with nothing dropped.

```
2026-10-24 22:45:30 [INFO] === DB up: consume TXN-1, TXN-2 normally ===
```

```text
  Wire: {"txnId":"TXN-1","accountId":"SAV2001","amount":20000}  (bytes)
    │
    ▼
  ErrorHandlingDeserializer → JsonDeserializer
    │ check type com.bank.settlement.model.TxnEvent ∈ trusted.packages
    │ Jackson → TxnEvent{txnId, accountId, amount:BigDecimal}
    ▼
  ListenerControl.deliver(event)
    │
    ├─ DB UP ──────────────→ SettlementListener.onTxn() → settle
    │
    └─ DB DOWN:

             ▼

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka stores values as raw bytes, so a deserializer is what turns those bytes back into an object on the consumer side. The raw client's default is the byte array deserializer, and a typical Spring setup defaults to the string deserializer, which just gives you the JSON as text to parse yourself. To consume JSON as a strongly typed object I set the value deserializer to Spring Kafka's JsonDeserializer, which uses Jackson to reconstruct the payload directly into my target type, so the listener method receives a ready-made object instead of a string.

Two settings make that safe. I tell the deserializer the target type, either a default type or a type stamped in a message header by the producer, and I configure trusted packages as an allowlist of the packages it is permitted to instantiate. Trusted packages matters for security, because without it a malicious producer could stamp a dangerous type header and trick the deserializer into building an unexpected class; I name my own packages explicitly and never use a wildcard in production. I also wrap the JsonDeserializer in an ErrorHandlingDeserializer so one malformed payload becomes a recoverable error that goes to a dead letter topic instead of poisoning the partition.

For runtime flow control I use dynamic pause and resume. I give the listener an id, inject the KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry, look up the container by id, and call pause or resume on it. When paused, the container keeps the consumer alive, holds its partition assignment, and keeps heartbeating, so it does not cause a rebalance, but it stops delivering records to my method and the offsets stay put.

In the settlement service at National Bank of India this was exactly how we handled database maintenance. A health indicator watched the account database, and when it went down it paused the listener so we stopped consuming events we could not settle, which froze the offsets and avoided a storm of transient failures flooding the dead letter topic. When the database came back, it resumed the listener and we picked up precisely where we had stopped, settling Rajesh's and Priya's held transfers in their original order with nothing lost. The senior point I stress is that pausing is far healthier than letting a listener keep failing, because it holds position cleanly without burning retries or risking the consumer being evicted from the group.
